title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Roof soft washing
audience: Roof soft washing owners and team leads who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a roof cleaning need may be starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what roof work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the roof types you soft-wash well, the price range you can sustain, the postcodes you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each client needs you. A route of single-storey homes you can reach in one day is worth more to a small business than one difficult job across town. The lead-generation guide's soft-wash typical for a single-storey house is $480 (What's The Damage, verified November 2026), but that is an estimate and not evidence of how often roofs are bought in your area.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list, and be plain about the evidence
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using written criteria: service area, repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the roof falls within your licence and insurance. Owners corporations can be a route, because Consumer Victoria says an owners corporation manages common property. Whether a roof is common property depends on the plan, and the research found no roof-specific owners corporation evidence. Real-estate offices, insurers and solar installers are also candidates, but this research found no evidence for any of them, so treat them as segments to test. Use only contact details published for business use, record the date and source of each entry, and do not use bought or harvested lists. A building permit dataset may show area-level activity, but it does not confirm owner or builder names, so use it for planning only.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals, and use them for timing only
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a roof need more likely soon. Examples include a planning application for alterations on a street where you already work, a planned works notice for a common area, or a change of occupier at a site you already service. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. The City of Casey planning permit register on Victoria's open data portal shows application status and suburb; check your own council's register. The Victorian building permit dataset records location, estimated cost and issue date, and can be filtered by suburb or postcode, but the research could not confirm whether it records roof works. Do not monitor private people, do not enter a property without an invitation, and do not go to a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you learned of the notice or the business, makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or the business's own published material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for one defined roof. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling found many approaches were pressured or misleading, that about 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. A specific, honest message that names you is a practical advantage as well as a compliance step. Where the message goes by email or text, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, then a pause. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the roof types, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and the source of its contact details.
Choose two or three public signals to watch, and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and your licence and insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A roof soft washer sees a roof with visible staining from the footpath in a street where he already works. He considers knocking on doors along the street to offer a clean.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should he go door to door, and what should he do instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: He should not turn up at the homes to make an offer. The research says not to go to a home to make an offer, and the ACCC's 2026 findings describe pressured and misleading approaches as widespread. He can use a route the owner has agreed to: a business or owners corporation contact published for business use, or a written offer to the owner in a way that the electronic message rules allow. He records the signal and its date, and does not contact individual residents using private details. If the street has an active planning application, the signal is about the application, not about the residents. He checks his licence and insurance for roof work before any message goes out.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any roof visit follows the Victorian working-at-height method and the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Going door to door to offer a roof clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not turn up at a home to make an offer. Use a route the recipient has agreed to, or a published business contact.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. In Victoria, a soft wash alone appears outside the roofing licence scope, while gutter and downpipe work appears inside it; that reading is not confirmed. Licence rules differ between states and territories. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Public information does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is unconfirmed here.

Victoria: the working-at-height rule for roofs was not checked in this draft. WorkSafe Victoria says allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident. Check the Victorian rule before quoting any roof access.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the roof work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals for timing, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and do not door-knock. Owners corporation, insurer and solar-installer prospects are untested.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A planning notice shows works on a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for a roof clean
Go into the common area to look at the roof before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include a free unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some others. The page as read lists the APP chapters only; small-business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: OAIC.
